t:
(a) In General.—Section 984 of title 18, United States Code, is amended— 
    (1) by striking subsection (a) and redesignating subsections (b), (c), and (d) as subsections (a), (b), and (c), respectively; 
    (2) in subsection (a), as redesignated—

        (A) by striking “or other fungible property” and inserting “or precious metals”; and 
        (B) in paragraph (2), by striking “subsection (c)” and inserting “subsection (b)”;  
    (3) in subsection (c), as redesignated—

        (A) by striking paragraph (1) and inserting the following; “(1) Subsection (a) does not apply to an action against funds held by a financial institution in an interbank account unless the account holder knowingly engaged in the offense that is the basis for the forfeiture.”; and 
        (B) in paragraph (2), by striking “(2) As used in this section, the term” and inserting the following:

“(2) In this subsection—
“(A) the term ‘financial institution’ includes a foreign bank (as defined in section 1(b)(7) of the International Banking Act of 1978 (12 U.S.C. 3101(b)(7))); and
“(B) the term”; and
  
    (4) by adding at the end the following:

“(d) Nothing in this section may be construed to limit the ability of the Government to forfeit property under any provision of law if the property involved in the offense giving rise to the forfeiture or property traceable thereto is available for forfeiture.”.

fable.w: This section makes technical amendments to the civil forfeiture statute for fungible property, redesignating subsections and defining terms. The tempting reading is that the reference to an "action against funds" involves litigation, but that is a forfeiture action brought by the Government, not a right for an outside party to sue over or object to a federal decision. Nothing here provides for consultation, comment, hearings, advisory bodies, or rulemaking involving non-federal parties.
fable.s: Subsection (a) does not apply to an action against funds held by a financial institution in an interbank account unless the account holder knowingly engaged in the offense that is the basis for the forfeiture.

opus.w: This section makes technical changes to the civil forfeiture statute (18 U.S.C. 984): it redesignates subsections, changes the scope from fungible property to precious metals, and limits forfeiture of interbank accounts. The 'action' it mentions is a government forfeiture action, not a right for an outside party to challenge a federal decision. No one outside the federal government is consulted or brought into a decision, and no rulemaking or hearing is required.
opus.s: Subsection (a) does not apply to an action against funds held by a financial institution in an interbank account unless the account holder knowingly engaged in the offense that is the basis for the forfeiture.
opus.b: 1. **Tempting reading:** The text mentions "an action against funds" and forfeiture proceedings, which could look like litigation rights. That reading fails. These are civil forfeiture actions brought by the government. The section does not give any outside party a right to sue over or object to a federal decision, and it creates no consultation, hearing, comment period, advisory body or rulemaking.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends criminal forfeiture laws regarding property and funds. It does not require the government to consult with outside entities like financial institutions before making a decision; rather, it defines the scope of property subject to forfeiture. The interaction described is adversarial (forfeiture), not participatory (consultation/advisory).
qwen_chat.s: (d) Nothing in this section may be construed to limit the ability of the Government to forfeit property under any provision of law if the property involved in the offense giving rise to the forfeiture or property traceable thereto is available for forfeiture.
qwen_chat.b:
Temptation: The text mentions "financial institutions" and "foreign banks," which are outside entities, and discusses legal actions against them.
Resolution: This section amends criminal forfeiture laws regarding property and funds. It does not require the government to consult with these entities before making a decision; rather, it defines the scope of property subject to forfeiture. The interaction described is adversarial (forfeiture), not participatory (consultation/advisory).
